title: Climate finance

definition.text: Money, such as loans, grants or government budget spending, used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience.

facts.text: The money can come from private or public sources and can pass through intermediaries such as multilateral development banks and development agencies.
Under the UN Climate Convention, climate finance means transfers of public money from high-income to low- and middle-income countries, in line with their duty to provide new and additional resources.
It has two main subcategories: mitigation finance, which aims to reduce emissions, and adaptation finance, which responds to the consequences of climate change.
Global climate finance was estimated at around $1.3 trillion per year in 2021/2022, up from more than US$600 billion in 2019 by one estimate.
Most of it, 84% in 2021/2022, is raised and spent within the same country.
A 2024 report estimated that flows must rise at least sixfold on 2021/2022 levels, to $8.5 trillion per year by 2030.
Public budgets are widely seen as too small to meet the need, so private finance is expected to be important for closing the gap.
Its main challenges are measuring and tracking flows, fair support for developing countries, and giving private investors suitable incentives.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
related: New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance

definition.text: Investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: Mitigation accounts for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance.
Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to renewable energy; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors.
Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation.
The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.
The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year.

definition.text: Climate finance that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: It comes from governments, development finance institutions and multilateral climate funds, and from private sources such as banks, investors, companies and households.
Around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources, partly because adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return.
Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation.
Benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion.
A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030.
Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.

title: Adaptation finance gap
article: Climate finance#Current levels of financing and the finance gap

definition.text: The difference between the estimated cost of adapting to climate change and the money available for adaptation.

facts.text: International public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year between 2017 and 2021.
On 2017–2021 data, estimated needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments.
A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans estimated developing countries' adaptation needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030.
More public and private finance, remittances and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed could help close it.

definition.text: The shortfall between the climate investment that is needed and what is actually provided.

facts.text: Estimates of the gap vary with the places, sectors, timescale, target and assumptions used.
Research finds bilateral climate finance well below official figures, partly because there is no agreed definition of international climate finance and no oversight.
This has let non-climate projects be counted and raised doubts about official reporting.

definition.text: Funds governed by several national governments together that pay out money for climate action.

facts.text: As of 2022, the UNFCCC coordinated five: the Green Climate Fund, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund, the Special Climate Change Fund and the Global Environment Facility.
The World Bank coordinates the Climate Investment Funds, active since 2008, made up of the Clean Technology Fund and the Strategic Climate Fund.
Some give only grants; others also use concessional loans, equity and risk tools meant to crowd in other finance.
In 2016 the four main multilateral climate funds approved $2.78 billion of project support.

definition.text: Climate investment from private sources such as banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households.

facts.text: Public budgets are often too small for large infrastructure projects, especially in lower-income countries, so private money is seen as needed to cover the shortfall.
Climate-friendly projects can cost more up front and carry more risk than fossil-fuel ones, so they must be bankable to attract private investors.
Over 90% of private climate flows are estimated to stay within national borders.
The IMF and OECD warn that private capital alone cannot close the gap, since many adaptation and innovation projects bring high social benefits but low private returns.

definition.text: A deal in which a country's debt is repaid on new discounted terms and the repayments, in local currency, are redirected to domestic climate projects.

facts.text: Projects funded this way can include carbon sequestration, renewable energy and conservation of biodiversity and oceans.
In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work.
Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism in a similar debt-for-nature swap.

title: Green Climate Fund

definition.text: A climate finance fund set up under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation.

facts.text: It is considered the world's largest fund of its kind and is the largest of the five multilateral climate funds coordinated by the UNFCCC.
It was named in the 2009 Copenhagen Accord, formally established at the 2010 Cancun conference, and its governing instrument was adopted in Durban in 2011.
It is based in Songdo, South Korea, and governed by a 24-member board with a secretariat.
As of November 2026 its portfolio was over $22.3 billion USD, or over $87.1 billion USD including co-financing.

One of its most controversial features is the Private Sector Facility: many rich countries want it to attract institutional investors, while developing countries and NGOs want pro-poor finance for small firms.
In March 2015 its board refused an explicit ban on fossil fuel projects, effectively allowing coal plants to be funded.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
contested_note: Rich and developing countries disagree over whether its private-sector arm should court large investors or support small firms, and over relying on private rather than pledged public money.

definition.text: The rule that climate finance given to developing countries should be new money, additional to existing development aid.

facts.text: The Cancun agreements require such finance, including through the Green Climate Fund, to be new and additional.
New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years.
There is no strict definition of additionality, which has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging CDM emission reductions.

title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: The international treaty, and the UN process built on it, through which countries negotiate how to limit dangerous climate change.

facts.text: It was signed by 154 states at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro and entered into force in 1994.
Its ultimate aim, in Article 2, is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system.
It set the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, with developed countries expected to lead because of their larger historical emissions.
By 2022 it had 198 parties, and its supreme body, the Conference of the Parties, meets every year.
Its work now centres on carrying out the Paris Agreement, which entered into force in 2016.
Decisions are taken by consensus, giving any party a veto, and it has been criticised as unsuccessful at cutting emissions.

title: Ultimate objective of the UNFCCC
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Interpreting ultimate objective in Article 2

definition.text: The UNFCCC's Article 2 goal of stabilising greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate.

facts.text: Article 2 says this should happen fast enough to let ecosystems adapt naturally, keep food production safe and let economic development continue sustainably.
Stabilising concentrations requires global emissions to peak and then decline, and earlier for lower stabilisation levels.
Science can describe climate risks, but deciding which risks count as dangerous needs value judgements.
Following the precautionary principle, acknowledged in Article 3, uncertainty about climate effects is no reason for inaction.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Annex I and non-Annex I countries
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Classification of Parties and their commitments

definition.text: The UNFCCC's grouping of countries into industrialised and transition economies (Annex I), richer donor countries (Annex II) and mostly developing countries (non-Annex I), each with different duties.

facts.text: There are 43 Annex I parties, including the EU; 14 of them are economies in transition, the former Soviet-bloc economies.
Annex I countries should adopt national policies to limit their emissions and report on returning to their 1990 levels.
The 24 Annex II parties are OECD members who must give financial and technical support to transition economies and developing countries.
49 parties are least-developed countries with special status, and developing countries may volunteer to join Annex I once sufficiently developed.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Kyoto Protocol

definition.text: An international treaty extending the UNFCCC that committed its parties to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: It was adopted in Kyoto on 11 December 1997 and entered into force on 16 February 2005.
Its main feature was legally binding emission-cut commitments for Annex I (industrialised) parties, based on common but differentiated responsibilities.
It covered seven gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide; the first commitment period ran from 2008 to 2012.

The 36 fully participating countries pledged a 4% aggregate cut from 1990 and achieved emissions 24.2% below 1990 in 2008–2012, largely thanks to the Soviet Union's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis.
Even so, global emissions rose by 32% from 1990 to 2010, since the committed countries made up only 24% of global emissions in 2010.
The United States never ratified it and Canada withdrew effective December 2012.
It was followed in 2015 by the Paris Agreement, a separate instrument under the UNFCCC rather than an amendment.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
Annex I and non-Annex I countries

title: Criticism of the Kyoto Protocol

definition.text: The debate over whether the Kyoto Protocol's commitments were too weak, too costly, or wrongly designed.

facts.text: Some environmentalists and scientists found its commitments too weak, while several economists thought them stronger than justified.
Stavins called it 'too little, too fast', and Stern said its lack of a long-term goal kept it from sending a credible signal.
Critics objected that it set cuts only for rich countries and none for fast-growing economies such as China and India.
Nordhaus argued its quantity-type instruments were less efficient than price-type ones and that it might be better redesigned as a global carbon tax.

contested_note: Sources disagree over whether Kyoto's commitments were too weak or too strong, and whether its quantity-based design was sound.

definition.text: The large surplus of Kyoto emission allowances held by former Soviet-bloc economies, whose sale would not actually cut emissions.

facts.text: Russia, Ukraine and the new EU-12 states had surplus allowances because their emissions targets were set above their actual emissions.
These transition economies saw the surplus as 'headroom' to grow their economies.
Countries short of allowances could buy them from those with a surplus, but without further commitments this trade would not reduce emissions.

definition.text: The Kyoto Protocol's system for monitoring whether parties meet their commitments and penalising those that do not.

facts.text: A party that misses its emissions limit must make up the difference in the second commitment period plus an additional 30%.
It is also suspended from making transfers under emissions trading.
Grubb judged the treaty's consequences for non-compliance weak compared with domestic law, and the compliance section was hotly contested in the Marrakesh Accords.

definition.text: The 2012 extension of the Kyoto Protocol that set a second commitment period running to 2020.

facts.text: It was agreed on 8 December 2012 in Doha, with 37 countries holding binding targets, and set 2015 as the date for a successor agreement.
Japan, New Zealand and Russia took on no new targets, and the second period covered only about 11% of global annual emissions.
It entered into force on 31 December 2020, after 144 states accepted it, on the very day the second period ended.

title: Copenhagen Accord

definition.text: A 2009 agreement produced by a group of countries at the Copenhagen climate conference, which the conference only 'took note of'.

facts.text: It said global warming should be limited to below 2.0 °C, which the UNFCCC reads as relative to pre-industrial temperatures.
114 countries agreed to it, and 17 developed parties plus the EU-27 and 45 developing parties submitted mitigation targets.
It set the goal of sending $100 billion a year to developing countries by 2020 and proposed the Green Climate Fund.
The conference had been seen as the chance to agree a successor to Kyoto.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
notes: No page of its own in the crawl; the Copenhagen climate summit page was fetched but is in no dossier.

title: Cancún agreements

definition.text: Decisions taken at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún, including national mitigation pledges and the creation of the Green Climate Fund.

facts.text: They included voluntary pledges from 76 developed and developing countries, which together produced 85% of global annual emissions in 2010.
Parties agreed that future warming should stay below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.
Developed countries committed to jointly mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
They require climate finance to developing countries to be 'new' and 'additional' to existing aid.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Criticism of the UNFCCC process
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Criticism of processes

definition.text: The argument that the UNFCCC and Kyoto Protocol have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended.

facts.text: With over 190 countries deciding by consensus, small groups of countries can often block progress.
Japan refused a second Kyoto term in 2010 because it would face limits its competitors China, India and Indonesia did not.
The UNFCCC also failed, mainly under Kyoto, to transfer environmentally sound technologies to developing countries.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
contested_note: Critics call the consensus process ineffective, while historical responsibility for emissions remains a contentious issue in the talks.

title: Action for Climate Empowerment
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Six priority areas (Action for Climate Empowerment)

definition.text: The UNFCCC's name, adopted in 2015, for its work on climate education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information and cooperation on these.

facts.text: It refers to Article 6 of the 1992 convention text.
It calls on governments to run education and awareness programmes, train experts, open up information and promote public participation.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: National communication (UNFCCC)
article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#National communication

definition.text: A report that each country party to the UNFCCC submits on its climate measures and vulnerabilities.

facts.text: Developed countries must submit one every four years; developing countries should do so.
They are often several hundred pages long, while the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement are shorter and less detailed.
Some least developed countries have not submitted one in 5–15 years, mostly for lack of capacity.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Article 6 cooperative mechanisms
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: The part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their nationally determined contributions.

facts.text: It aims to allow higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation while promoting sustainable development, on condition of environmental integrity, transparency and robust accounting.
It has three pathways: cooperative approaches that trade ITMOs (6.2), a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4) and non-market approaches (6.8).
The core 'Article 6 rulebook' was adopted at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, and later decisions have focused on putting it into practice.
It succeeds the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, with the transition expected to be completed by 2025.
Its impact is debated, especially over environmental integrity, governance capacity and the risk of over-crediting.

contested_note: Analysts debate whether Article 6 transfers mainly lower costs and mobilise finance or undermine integrity through over-crediting, weak baselines and 'hot air'.

title: Internationally transferred mitigation outcomes
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.2: Cooperative approaches

definition.text: Measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement and that count toward the buyer's NDC.

facts.text: Article 6.2 lets countries trade them through bilateral or multilateral deals without using the central crediting mechanism.
They can be expressed in tonnes of CO2-equivalent or other metrics, and can come from crediting projects or from linked emissions trading systems.
By 2024 over 80 bilateral agreements were in place; the first completed trade, between Thailand and Switzerland, was reported in January 2024.

contested_note: Commentators disagree on whether these transfers mainly cut costs or risk over-crediting and 'hot air'.

title: Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (Article 6.4)

definition.text: A UN-supervised scheme set up under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals.

facts.text: Its credits are called Article 6.4 emission reductions (A6.4ERs) and are tracked in a registry with unique identifiers.
A share of proceeds goes to the Adaptation Fund, and a portion of units is cancelled to deliver an overall mitigation in global emissions.
Activities are validated, registered, monitored and independently verified before units are issued, under the oversight of the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body.

title: Non-market approaches (Article 6.8)
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.8: Non-market approaches

definition.text: Voluntary cooperation between countries under Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement that involves no international transfer of emission reductions.

facts.text: They can combine mitigation and adaptation and involve finance, technology transfer and capacity building.
A work programme and the Glasgow Committee on Non-market Approaches were set up at COP26 in 2021; the committee began work in 2022.

title: Corresponding adjustment
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Accounting, reporting and transparency architecture

definition.text: The accounting step that makes sure an emission reduction transferred between countries is counted in only one country's NDC.

facts.text: It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit.
Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this shows up in their NDC accounting.
Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

definition.text: A country's own pledge, under the Paris Agreement, of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change.

facts.text: NDCs are described as being at the heart of the Paris Agreement; each country decides for itself what to contribute.
They must be renewed every five years, and each should be more ambitious than the last, a rule called the principle of progression.
The pledges themselves are not binding, but preparing, communicating and updating them is; there is no way to force a country to meet its target.
Some pledges are unconditional, while others depend on outside finance, technical support or other countries' ambition.
They are the first UNFCCC emission targets that apply equally to developed and developing countries.
Emission cuts must rise 80% beyond current NDCs to likely meet 2 °C; on current trends the chance of staying below 2 °C is only 5%.

definition.text: The initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges countries made before the 2015 Paris Agreement, which became their first NDCs.

facts.text: UNFCCC parties were asked to publish them at the 2013 Warsaw climate conference.
The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones.
Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015; 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

title: Ratchet mechanism

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges, designed to raise countries' climate ambition over time.

facts.text: Countries publish biennial progress reports that undergo technical review.
These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all NDCs together are enough.
The stocktake's findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

notes: Title 'Ratchet mechanism' is a common name; the cited section speaks of a framework 'designed to ratchet up climate action over time'.

title: Paris Agreement

definition.text: An international climate treaty, negotiated in 2015 and signed in 2016, covering mitigation, adaptation and finance.

facts.text: It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and preferably to 1.5 °C, with emissions reaching net zero by mid-century.
It was negotiated by 196 parties at the 2015 UN climate conference near Paris and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
Each country sets its own contributions, and each new target should go beyond the last, though nothing forces a country to set a specific target.
Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, it blurs the line between developed and developing countries, so developing countries must also submit emission-cut plans.
The EU and 194 states, covering over 98% of greenhouse gas emissions, have ratified or joined it; the United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026.
It recognises loss and damage as a separate pillar, but states it cannot be used as a basis for liability.
Global emissions kept rising after it was signed, and most experts say it is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Effectiveness of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: The debate over whether the Paris Agreement can achieve its temperature goals.

facts.text: Most experts say it is insufficient for the 1.5 °C goal, though some argue it is too early to judge.
UNEP said in 2020 that current commitments would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100.
Studies in Nature found that as of 2017 none of the major industrialised nations was implementing its pledged policies.
The stocktake report credits it with a large effect: the expected 2100 warming fell from 3.7–4.8 °C in 2010 to 2.4–2.6 °C at COP 27.

contested_note: Most experts judge the agreement insufficient for 1.5 °C, while others point to the drop in projected warming since it was adopted.

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's common system, under Article 13, for monitoring, reporting and verifying what countries do on climate and the support they give or receive.

facts.text: Parties are legally bound to have their progress toward their NDCs checked by technical expert review.
Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review.
It has built-in flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

definition.text: The international policy goal of keeping global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels.

facts.text: It is a political decision based on science about the likely consequences of warming, dating from the 2009 Copenhagen conference, and is central to the Paris Agreement.
It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature.
The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss.
The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100, exceeding the target.
An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down by late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

title: Climate club

definition.text: A voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members.

facts.text: Membership is voluntary and excludable, avoiding the need for every country to agree.
Countries join for the shared benefit of lower global emissions and to escape sanctions, such as tariffs, imposed on outsiders.
William Nordhaus pioneered the idea in 2015: members price carbon and charge a fee on imports from countries without similar pricing.
A 2025 Econometrica paper found such a club, with border taxes to deter free-riding, could achieve 33–68% of the globally optimal carbon reduction.
The G7 Climate Club, launched in December 2022, favours partnerships over penalties and had 46 member states as of May 2025.
Exporting countries fearing fees and researchers sceptical of carbon pricing have criticised it; the EU's CBAM has been called a possible first climate club.

contested_note: Critics fear export fees and doubt carbon pricing, while others argue supposed losers such as China and India would gain.

title: Climate debt

definition.text: The debt said to be owed by developed countries to developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions.

facts.text: It is part of the broader idea of ecological debt and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s.
Its two main parts are adaptation debt, help owed for adapting to climate change, and emissions debt, owed for excessive past emissions.
It gained attention at the 2009 Copenhagen conference, where developing countries led by Bolivia sought its repayment.
Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs; criticism comes mostly from developed nations.
Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts.
Some say that, even if ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

contested_note: Developing countries and NGOs press for climate debt to be repaid, while developed nations and some analysts reject the idea that a debt is owed.

definition.text: The part of climate debt said to be owed by developed countries for having used more than their fair share of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions.

facts.text: The atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions is called the total carbon space; the claim is that rich countries overused their fair allocation of it.
Since around 1750 the United States alone has produced 25% of all carbon emissions, and developed countries together 70%.
Repayment would mean helping poorer countries industrialise cleanly and sharing out the remaining carbon space by population.

definition.text: The compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that poorer nations suffer the worst consequences of a problem they did little to cause.
Lacking infrastructure and capital, poor countries often borrow at higher interest to recover from disasters, worsening their prospects.
The UNFCCC notes it can be met through financial aid and help coping with natural disasters.

title: Climate reparations

definition.text: Requested loss-and-damage payments for harm caused by climate change, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions and possibly including debt cancellation.

facts.text: Unlike plain 'loss and damage', the term treats compensation as an ethical and moral obligation that holds countries accountable for past emissions.
A 2023 study estimated that the top 21 fossil fuel companies will owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative reparations over 2025–2050.
Proposed channels include an international compensation commission, lawsuits, the polluter pays principle, debt forgiveness and direct grants.
The wealthiest nations have consistently opposed it at the UNFCCC, and before COP27 talks were steered to 'cooperation and facilitation' rather than liability.

contested_note: Developing nations and campaigners press for reparations, while rich nations oppose them and some argue current generations are not responsible for past emissions.

definition.text: A measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy, also called a climate goal or pledge, aimed at limiting climate change.

facts.text: Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming, and these underpin carbon budgets and emission targets.
At least 164 countries have climate targets in their national legislation.
Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
An emissions target may differ from a scientific carbon budget, since it can reflect political palatability rather than a specific temperature limit.
Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions, and many rely on negative-emission technologies not yet developed.

title: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities

definition.text: The principle, set in the 1992 UN climate convention, that all countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage but not to the same degree.

facts.text: Because developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation.
It can be seen as based on the polluter pays principle, with historical contribution and ability to act as the measures of responsibility.
Article 3 of the UNFCCC says developed countries should take the lead in combating climate change.
Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits; under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change.
Critics argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage; developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
related: Annex I and non-Annex I countries
contested_note: Some, including US negotiators, argue the rich–poor split is outdated or unfair, while developing countries defend it.

definition.text: A proposed global framework that shrinks total greenhouse gas emissions to a safe level while bringing every country's emissions per person to the same level.

facts.text: It was conceived by the Global Commons Institute in the early 1990s and is expressed as a simple mathematical formula.
Emission entitlements start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated rate of convergence.
Earlier convergence gives more entitlements to low-emitting, typically poorer, countries; the rate is described as a key equity lever.
Critics say a per-person basis could reward population growth, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

definition.text: Pressuring institutions to sell off stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change.

facts.text: It began on US university campuses in 2011, and by 2015 was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history.
As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of divestment.
Divesters act to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk.
One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off.
Its aim is to speed the renewable energy transition by stigmatising fossil fuel companies.
Fossil fuel companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for their rising cost of capital.

definition.text: The agreement reached at the 2021 UN climate conference (COP26) in Glasgow.

facts.text: It was the first climate agreement explicitly planning to reduce unabated coal use.
A pledge to 'phase out' coal was changed late in the talks to 'phase down', at the urging of coal-reliant countries such as India and China.
Countries agreed to revisit their emission plans in 2022 to keep the 1.5 °C target within reach, and committed to climate finance for developing countries.
Around it, more than 140 countries had pledged net-zero emissions and more than 100 pledged to reverse deforestation by 2030.

title: Global climate regime

definition.text: The worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate system, in order to limit climate change.

facts.text: Its framework was set by the UNFCCC, and its first legally binding result was the Kyoto Protocol.
Between 2013 and 2015 there was no legally binding global climate regime, and the voluntary Copenhagen Accord pledges served in practice.
The 2015 Paris Agreement became the regime, with all countries signed on to balancing greenhouse gas sources and sinks in the second half of the century.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly review of how far the world as a whole has got toward the agreement's goals.

facts.text: It links countries' NDCs to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next NDCs to raise ambition.
It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out.
After debate, it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance.
It runs in three phases: collecting information, technical assessment, and political messages for policy.
The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

definition.text: The first Paris Agreement stocktake, concluded at COP 28 in Dubai in December 2023 as part of the UAE Consensus.

facts.text: It found pledges insufficient: a 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected.
It set 2030 targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double global energy efficiency.
For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050.
It set up the loss and damage fund with $700 million in start-up capital, to be administered by the World Bank.

definition.text: A usually public or quasi-public financial institution that works with private investors to speed up the spread of clean energy technologies.

facts.text: It uses public funds to leverage private investment in clean technologies that are commercially viable but slow to spread.
It lowers risk for private investors through tools such as concessional finance, guarantees, credit enhancement, co-investment and securitisation.
Its public capital can be reinvested again and again across many clean energy projects.
The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allotted $27 billion to green banks through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund.

title: History of climate change policy
article: History of climate change policy and politics

definition.text: The history of political actions, policies, controversies and activism concerning climate change.

facts.text: Formal global environmental politics began with the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm.
The first World Climate Conference in 1979 framed climate change as a global political issue, and the IPCC was set up in 1988.
Efforts have mostly sought consensus at the UN under the UNFCCC, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol cited as a precedent that this can work.
Critics of this top-down approach propose bottom-up governance instead.
Adaptation was long seen as a distraction from mitigation and gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder.
Climate policy became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s, with the US partisan gap the widest in history in 2020.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: An international treaty that protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it.

facts.text: It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989.
With 198 parties it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history and is often called the most successful international environmental agreement.
Developing countries get extra time to comply under Article 5, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them.
Concentrations of the main CFCs have levelled off or fallen, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly recovering.
It has also benefited climate change mitigation; HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases.
It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

definition.text: A 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol under which countries promised to cut their use of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by more than 80% over 30 years.

facts.text: It came into force on 1 January 2019.
HFCs replaced CFCs and do not harm the ozone layer, but they are greenhouse gases with a high global warming potential.
A 2009 study calculated that a fast HFC phasedown could avoid up to 8.8 Gt CO2-eq per year of emissions by 2050.

definition.text: The fund that helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with the Montreal Protocol.

facts.text: It serves countries using less than 0.3 kg of ozone-depleting substances per person a year; 147 of the 196 parties qualify.
It embodies the principle of common but differentiated responsibility to protect the global commons.
It is run by an executive committee with equal numbers of industrialised and developing countries, the first such democratically managed treaty fund.

title: ICJ advisory opinion on climate obligations
article: Obligations of States in respect of climate change

definition.text: A 2025 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice on what international law requires states to do to protect the climate, requested by the UN General Assembly in 2023.

facts.text: The request, led by Vanuatu and driven by Pacific island students, was adopted by the General Assembly by consensus on 29 March 2023.
The Court unanimously held that the UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement create binding obligations, including submitting NDCs and acting on common but differentiated responsibilities.
Failing to meet these obligations is an internationally wrongful act that can require cessation, guarantees of non-repetition and full reparation, given a clear causal link.
Because the climate is a global common good, any state may invoke another's responsibility for breaches; the opinion is not binding but is expected to be used in courts.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Pledge and review

definition.text: A way of organising international climate action in which each country makes its own pledge, others review its progress, and stronger pledges follow.

facts.text: It is a 'bottom-up' approach, unlike legally binding targets imposed 'top-down' by a central body.
Japan first proposed it in 1991; it was rejected at the first COP in 1995 in favour of binding targets, which led to the Kyoto Protocol.
Revived at Copenhagen in 2009, it drew pledges from countries producing about 80% of global emissions, versus 25% covered by Kyoto's first targets.
By 2015 it was the central approach, though at Paris the pledges were renamed Nationally Determined Contributions.
It became dominant because binding greenhouse-gas targets proved hard to agree and impossible to enforce on powerful nations.
Critics called it 'hedge and retreat' or 'second best', while others called it an essential pillar of mitigation.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
contested_note: Environmental groups and some academics have called pledge-and-review inadequate, while other academics see it as essential.

definition.text: A loan with an interest rate below the market rate.

facts.text: It may also offer other concessions, such as long repayment periods or interest holidays.
Governments usually give soft loans to projects they consider worthwhile, and the World Bank and other development institutions give them to developing countries.
Some official development assistance is counted as the concessional value of soft loans.

title: United Nations Climate Change Conference

definition.text: The yearly conferences, known as COPs, at which the parties to the UN climate convention meet to assess and negotiate climate action.

facts.text: The first, COP 1, was held in Berlin in 1995.
Since 2005 they also serve as the meeting of the Kyoto Protocol's parties, and from 2011 to 2015 they were used to negotiate the Paris Agreement.
Any final text of a COP must be agreed by consensus.
Hosting rotates among the five UN regional groups.
More than 5,350 fossil fuel industry lobbyists attended the four conferences from 2021 to 2024.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Bali Action Plan
article: United Nations Climate Change Conference#2007: COP 13/CMP 3, Bali, Indonesia

definition.text: The 2007 decision at COP 13 in Bali that set a timeline and structure for negotiating a climate framework for after 2012.

facts.text: Developed countries agreed to comparable quantified emission targets, while developing countries agreed to nationally appropriate mitigation actions supported by technology, finance and capacity building.
It set up a new body, the Ad Hoc Working Group on Long-term Cooperative Action, for these negotiations, which ran through 2008 and 2009 toward Copenhagen.
The Bali conference also drew attention to the 20% of global emissions caused by deforestation.

title: New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance

definition.text: The new climate finance target, negotiated at COP29 in 2024, for supporting developing countries after 2025, building on the earlier $100 billion a year goal.

facts.text: The earlier goal, set in 2009 and agreed at Cancún in 2010, was for developed countries to mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
That target was missed in 2020 and reached only in 2022; an OECD report gave $132.8 billion in 2023 and $136.7 billion in 2024.
At COP29 in Baku, delegations agreed that developed nations would pledge $300 billion a year by 2035, from public and private sources.
Poorer nations called this insufficient and many pushed for at least $500 billion; some critics, including UN officials, called it a betrayal.
A key tension was the donor base: the US and EU wanted countries such as China and the Gulf states to contribute, but the text only encouraged voluntary contributions.
Talks at COP30 were expected to address scaling finance from the $300 billion agreed in Baku to $1.3 trillion.

contested_note: Developing countries and critics called the $300 billion figure too small, while developed countries pressed for a wider donor base.

title: Ozone depletion

definition.text: Ozone depletion is a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere plus a much larger springtime decrease over the polar regions, observed since the late 1970s.

facts.text: The main causes are manufactured halocarbons used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents (CFCs, HCFCs, halons), called ozone-depleting substances.
The ozone layer absorbs UVB light, so depletion raises surface UVB, which could increase skin cancer; this was the reason for the Montreal Protocol.

Since the Montreal Protocol was adopted and strengthened, concentrations of the most significant CFCs have declined; effective equivalent chlorine peaked in 1994 and had dropped about 10 percent by 2008.
The Vienna and Montreal conventions were put in place before a scientific consensus existed or key uncertainties were resolved.
Frank Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina suggested in 1974 that long-lived organic halogen compounds such as CFCs could deplete ozone.

related: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

title: Antarctic ozone hole
article: Ozone depletion#Ozone hole and its causes

definition.text: The Antarctic ozone hole is an area of the Antarctic stratosphere where ozone has dropped to as low as 33 percent of pre-1975 values.

facts.text: It occurs in the Antarctic spring, September to early December, when strong westerly winds form a polar vortex in which over 50 percent of lower stratospheric ozone is destroyed.
British Antarctic Survey scientists reported it in Nature in May 1985; the decline was far larger than anticipated.
It is measured as reduced total column ozone in Dobson units; actual hole values are in the 150-100 DU range.

title: Ozone-depleting substances
article: Ozone depletion#Observations on ozone layer depletion > Compounds in the atmosphere > CFCs and related compounds

definition.text: Ozone-depleting substances are halogenated chemicals, chiefly CFCs, that are mainly responsible for man-made ozone depletion.

facts.text: The total effective chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere is expressed as equivalent effective stratospheric chlorine (EESC).
Very short-lived substances, which degrade in under 6 months, are allowed by the Montreal Protocol; 90% are natural, 10% manmade such as dichloromethane.
CFCs are well mixed globally and are not kept from the stratosphere by their weight, since wind mixes atmospheric gases.

definition.text: The Global Environment Facility is a multilateral environmental fund giving grants and blended finance to developing countries for biodiversity, climate change, international waters, land degradation, pollutants and forests.

facts.text: It is the largest multilateral funder of biodiversity, distributing over $1 billion a year on average; it has provided more than $22 billion in grants and mobilized $120 billion in co-financing for over 5,200 projects.
It began in October 1991 as a $1 billion World Bank pilot and became a permanent separate institution at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; the World Bank has been trustee since 1994.
It is the financial mechanism for the CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention and Minamata Convention, and supports the Montreal Protocol.
Donors pledged a record $5.33 billion in June 2022 for the replenishment cycle running to June 2026.
Its Small Grants Programme supported nearly 27,000 civil society and community initiatives in 136 countries.

definition.text: The GEF funds the incremental or additional costs of turning a project with national benefits into one with global environmental benefits.

facts.text: The GEF provides new and additional grants and concessional funding to cover those incremental costs.

definition.text: The GEF is governed through an Assembly, a Council, a Secretariat, agencies, a scientific panel and an Independent Evaluation Office.

facts.text: The Assembly of all 184 member countries meets every three to four years at ministerial level.
The Council, the main governing body, has 32 members (14 developed, 16 developing, 2 transition economies), meets twice annually and decides by consensus.
The Independent Evaluation Office reports directly to the Council and evaluates GEF impact and effectiveness.
